title: Curved Spine and Morning Headaches / Chest Wall Failure Needs Night-Time Support

blocks.text: Curved Spine and Morning Headaches / Chest Wall Failure Needs Night-Time Support

AMaC MRCP PACES · R2-05 · Physical examination · PACES Station 1, respiratory examination · Skills A, B, D, E, G · 10 minutes (up to 6 minutes examining, then at least 4 minutes of examiner questions) · Guidelines: BTS Guideline for oxygen use in adults in healthcare and emergency settings (published 2017); DVLA Miscellaneous conditions: assessing fitness to drive (last updated 7 November 2025) · Related AMaC: AMaC COPD examination station; this one tests chest wall restriction and night-time hypoventilation
Ms Ingrid Lowther is 52 and works part-time as a librarian. She has had morning headaches and tiredness for a year, and she is breathless on walking. Please examine her respiratory system.
You may examine for up to 6 minutes. The examiners will then ask you questions.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. A curved spine, morning headaches and a flapping tremor mean the chest wall is failing at night. The lungs are healthy; the bellows are not.

The Examiner Trap. Candidates look for lung disease, find a clear chest, and miss the spine and the flap. Pass: kyphoscoliosis with carbon dioxide retention, tests, and night-time ventilation. Fail: oxygen alone.

rows: The spine is the finding. Look from behind and from the side before you listen.
"May I examine your chest and back? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable?"
Clean hands; introduce, consent; stand her to look at the spine, then sit her; hands, flap, pulse, face.
Chest wall disease: both sides move poorly, the lungs sound clear, and carbon dioxide shows in the hands.
"I'm going to tap and listen from the back, then ask you to hold your arms out."
Spine and rib hump; expansion; percussion; auscultation; flap; JVP; ankles; look for a cause; cover her; clean hands.
Name the deformity, then the failure it causes, then the night-time plan.
"She has severe kyphoscoliosis with signs of carbon dioxide retention. I'd test for night-time hypoventilation."
Present in order; diagnosis; investigations; ventilation service referral; driving advice; thank her.
Starts without consent; asks her to stand unsupported when unsteady; leaves her exposed.
Cleans hands, introduces self, consents, offers support to stand, sits her at 45 degrees, covers her afterwards.
Also offers a chaperone, keeps exposure to the minimum, and pauses if she is tired.
Listens to the front only; omits the spine, hands or flap.
Looks at the spine from behind and the side, then hands, flap, JVP, expansion, percussion and auscultation.
Also looks for a cause and checks the ankles.
Misses the spine, or reports crackles or wheeze that are not present.
Finds severe kyphoscoliosis with a right rib hump, reduced expansion on both sides, a flapping tremor and a full-volume pulse.
Also states a clear chest, no cyanosis, JVP not raised and no oedema, so no sign of right heart strain.
Kyphoscoliosis with type 2 respiratory failure from a restrictive chest wall.
Also states the likely cause is idiopathic with no neurofibromas or Marfan features, and lists obesity and neuromuscular causes.
Blood gas, spirometry with vital capacity, and overnight oximetry or a sleep study with carbon dioxide monitoring.
Also explains that the decision rests on symptoms plus daytime hypercapnia or nocturnal hypoventilation, with a falling vital capacity prompting closer sleep assessment.
Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): gives high-flow oxygen alone to a drowsy patient who retains carbon dioxide.
Refers to the home ventilation service for night-time non-invasive ventilation; uses controlled oxygen only, to 88-92%.
Also tells her drowsiness with a low saturation is an emergency needing a blood gas, senior help and ventilation.
Advises her not to drive while sleepy, until symptoms are controlled.
Also gives the 3-month rule for other medical causes, says the bus and lorry rule is the same, and says moderate or severe sleep apnoea means no driving and immediate notification to DVLA.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Not used for this station type.

Findings, released as each step is done: short trunk, comfortable at rest; respiratory rate 20; pulse 88, full volume; blood pressure 128/76; SpO2 91% on air; temperature 36.6 °C. Hands: warm, no clubbing; mild flapping tremor. Face: no cyanosis. Spine: severe thoracic kyphoscoliosis, convex to the right, rib hump on bending; no scars. Trachea central. Expansion reduced both sides; percussion resonant; breath sounds vesicular, quieter on the left; no crackles or wheeze. JVP not raised; no oedema. No neurofibromas, no spider fingers; feet normal.
Question ladder: 1. What do you see? (B) Kyphoscoliosis, flap, warm hands. 2. Diagnosis? (D) 3. Investigations? (E) 4. Treatment? (E) 5. She drives to work: advice? (E)
Curveball: She becomes drowsy; SpO2 is 84%. Controlled oxygen, blood gas, senior help, ventilation. Will oxygen alone help? No; it can worsen carbon dioxide retention.
Cleans hands, introduces self, gains consent and supports her standing (G)
Looks at the spine from behind and the side first (A)
Finds kyphoscoliosis, reduced expansion, and a flap with a full-volume pulse (B)
States a clear chest and no sign of right heart strain (B)
Names kyphoscoliosis with type 2 respiratory failure (D)
Requests blood gas, vital capacity and a sleep study (E)
Refers for night-time non-invasive ventilation (E)
Uses controlled oxygen only, to 88-92%, until gases are back (E)
Advises her not to drive while sleepy (E)
Covers her, cleans hands and thanks her (G)
Fail performance
CANDIDATE: Stand up for me. [R1 Fail]
CANDIDATE: (Listens at the front only.) [R2 Fail] There are crackles at the bases. [R3 Fail] It's COPD. [R4 Fail]
EXAMINER: Plan?
CANDIDATE: Chest X-ray. [R5 Fail] Give her high-flow oxygen. [R6 Fail] She can keep driving. [R7 Fail]

Examiner note: Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): high-flow oxygen can raise carbon dioxide in someone who is already retaining it. The spine and flap were missed, a sign was invented, and driving was ignored.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) Ms Lowther, I'm one of the doctors. May I examine your chest and back? Can I help you stand? Is this angle comfortable? [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: (Spine from behind and the side; hands, flap, JVP; expansion, percussion and auscultation.) [R2 Pass]
CANDIDATE: She has severe kyphoscoliosis with a right rib hump, reduced expansion on both sides, a flapping tremor and a full-volume pulse. [R3 Pass]
CANDIDATE: (Covers her, cleans hands.) Thank you. [R1 Pass]
EXAMINER: Diagnosis?
CANDIDATE: Kyphoscoliosis with type 2 respiratory failure from a restrictive chest wall. [R4 Pass]
EXAMINER: Investigations?
CANDIDATE: Blood gas, spirometry with vital capacity, and overnight oximetry or a sleep study with carbon dioxide monitoring. [R5 Pass]
EXAMINER: Treatment?
CANDIDATE: Refer to the home ventilation service for night-time non-invasive ventilation; controlled oxygen only, to 88-92%. [R6 Pass]
EXAMINER: She drives.
CANDIDATE: She must not drive while sleepy, until symptoms are controlled. [R7 Pass]
Examiner note: Safe and complete. Did not state the thresholds, the cause, the right heart check or the 3-month rule.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) Ms Lowther, may I examine your chest and back? Would you like a chaperone? I'll help you stand, keep you covered, and stop if you tire. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: (Spine; hands, flap, JVP; both sides from the back; ankles; skin and feet for a cause.) [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: Severe kyphoscoliosis with a right rib hump, reduced expansion, flap and full-volume pulse. A clear chest, no cyanosis, JVP not raised, no oedema. [R3 High]
CANDIDATE: (Covers her, cleans hands, thanks her.) [R1 High]
EXAMINER: Diagnosis?
CANDIDATE: Kyphoscoliosis with type 2 respiratory failure, probably idiopathic: no neurofibromas or Marfan features. Obesity and neuromuscular disease are the alternatives. [R4 High]
EXAMINER: Investigations?

CANDIDATE: Blood gas and a sleep study. The home ventilation service decides on night-time ventilation from her symptoms, daytime carbon dioxide and nocturnal hypoventilation; a low vital capacity makes me look harder but does not decide it alone. [R5 High]
EXAMINER: Treatment?
CANDIDATE: Home ventilation referral, controlled oxygen only. If she becomes drowsy with a low saturation: blood gas, senior help and ventilation. [R6 High]
EXAMINER: She drives.

CANDIDATE: Not while sleepy. DVLA must be told if the sleepiness is not controlled within 3 months, and the rule is the same for car and for bus or lorry licences. If a sleep study showed moderate or severe sleep apnoea she must stop driving and notify DVLA straight away. [R7 High]
Examiner note: Added the chaperone, the cause check, the right heart check, the basis for the ventilation decision, the emergency pathway and the 3-month rule.
R3: Missing the spine and flap. The diagnosis is visible from the back; without it the chest is just clear.
R4: Calling it COPD. The lungs are normal and the problem is the chest wall, so the plan targets the wrong organ.
R6: High-flow oxygen. In a patient already retaining carbon dioxide it can cause drowsiness and worse failure today.
R7: Silence about driving. Sleepiness behind the wheel can harm her and others.
"Let me look at her spine from behind before I go on."
"The chest is clear, so the problem is the chest wall, not the lungs."
"May I summarise what I found and give my diagnosis?"

Kyphoscoliosis restricts the chest wall and can cause night-time hypoventilation, then daytime carbon dioxide retention. Morning headache, sleepiness, warm hands, a flap and a full-volume pulse point to retention.

Home non-invasive ventilation is a specialist decision made on symptoms of hypoventilation (morning headache, sleepiness, breathlessness) together with daytime hypercapnia or nocturnal hypoventilation, for example nocturnal desaturation on overnight monitoring (commonly used criteria). A low vital capacity should prompt sleep and gas assessment but is not an automatic indication. Non-invasive ventilation is the established treatment for chest wall disease with chronic type 2 respiratory failure, started by a specialist ventilation service.

For people at risk of carbon dioxide retention, target saturations are 88-92% (BTS 2017). Excessive sleepiness from a medical condition: no driving until controlled; notify DVLA if not controlled within 3 months, for car and for bus or lorry licences alike. Moderate or severe sleep apnoea: no driving and notify DVLA immediately (DVLA, last updated 7 November 2025).
THINK: Clear chest, curved spine, flap: ventilation failure.
SAY: "Kyphoscoliosis with type 2 respiratory failure."
DO: Spine from behind first; look for the flap.
NUMBERS: Saturations 88-92% (BTS 2017). Ventilation is decided on symptoms plus hypercapnia or nocturnal hypoventilation, not on vital capacity alone (commonly used criteria).
TRAP: Looking for lung disease; high-flow oxygen.
FINISH: Night-time ventilation referral; no driving while sleepy.

BTS Guideline for oxygen use in adults in healthcare and emergency settings (published 2017). https://www.brit-thoracic.org.uk/quality-improvement/guidelines/emergency-oxygen/ Supports: Target saturation of 88-92% for people at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure.

DVLA. Miscellaneous conditions: assessing fitness to drive (last updated 7 November 2025). https://www.gov.uk/guidance/miscellaneous-conditions-assessing-fitness-to-drive Supports: No driving with excessive sleepiness until controlled; notify DVLA if not controlled within 3 months (same for Group 1 and Group 2); moderate or severe sleep apnoea means no driving and immediate notification.
